data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories inevitably smuggles induction back into Popper's system, rendering it internally inconsistent when transitioning from logical analysis to practical application, as any action based on past tests implicitly assumes the future will resemble the past.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If a form of rational action can be demonstrated that relies solely on negative elimination without any positive expectation of future outcomes.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If Popper's distinction between 'corroboration' (past) and 'prediction' (future) can be maintained strictly in the mind of the acting scientist.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the 'pragmatic' defense can be shown to be purely linguistic rather than operational.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The Inductive Leakage Mechanism: This mechanism argues that the act of 'preferring' for the sake of 'action' creates an inescapable pragmatic commitment to the predictive power of past tests. Even if labeled 'convention' or 'verisimilitude,' the psychological and functional reality of acting on a theory entails an expectation of future correspondence with reality, which is the definition of induction Popper sought to eliminate.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
